Lily Mine

By: Sasha OLD | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
3 people went in, and never came out. But what happened and how did it happen and what will happen next? Carte Blanche has exclusive access and will bring you shocking information 4 years on.

Unique Selling Point:
We have the miners. We have background sources. We have the documents necessary to show what happened on the day. We have amazing footage from the miners themselves, and those on the ground at the time. We also have amazing interviews with those that were there, and first hand accounts from family members of the victims. It's been 4 years, but the 3 victims are still down there - and from our documents it's likely they will never be recovered. We will answer, how this happened, examine the evidence and find out why this happened.

Extra Budget Items:
Stay:
Lily mine is near Lows Creek Barberton, Mpumalanga (about 1 hour 17 minutes from Nelspruit)
10-14th January (5 days, 4 nights) – stay with air bnb R2,751 for 4 nights at a lodge costing R599 per night, R355 service fee.

Travel:
Flights to Nelspruit: 1 person with return +-R3,000 pp. X 2 people, versus just one. Or I drive: roughly 450 there and back = (excl travel while there at R3.50 per/km) = R3,150 for petrol, The presenter can drive back with me as well.
Car hire 4 days and petrol: +-R550 per day car hire fee (4 days) = R2200 roughly

Production:
Graphic of lily mine falling R5,000.
Edit: 4 days with Floris: R3,600 X 4 = R14,400. 2 edit, view make changes, view and 1 online.
Okay I would need presenter: for 3 days. 2 days in Barberton (1 day work, 1 day travel) and 1 day for confronts in Johannesburg – depending on ROR.
Audio: depending on length of insert – could be 20 minutes, but obviously depends on what we have. It will be an epic – really could be a doccie.

For now we have the DMR report that nails the managers. We have sources at the mine that have been camping there – we can hear what’s been happening, the effort to help minors. We have our main source going on camera, and then we have the family members (3 families). We have the survivor stories, we have the stories of the town and how it’s failed.
We have confronts with Mike McChesney to do, intv with DMR. ROR from rescue practitioners, others named in report.
We have the graphic and to explain the years before the accident and the mess it’s been left in since.
2. Lily mine: I had asked you for feedback if I can send a camera man to interview Jan Haywood – the former mine shift leader who was cited in the report, and testified at the commission. He has the entire story, and can give us everything in detail on camera. It would cost R2,500 + petrol for camera man to go there and interview him? It’s R100km roughly from Durban. And Duncan Grant would film for me. As I doubt we would pay for me to go there, I can only skype him, and I think as someone who is speaking on the record it would be first prize to get this interview now and lock it down before they change their mind.

Press Release:


The anatomy of a mine collapse – what happened at Lily Mine?
It’s been four years of waiting in agony for the families of the three miners who never made it out of the collapsed Lily Mine in Barberton, Mpumalanga. Meanwhile, the Department of Mineral Resources has reached damning conclusions in an unpublished report into events and oversights that preceded the fatal collapse, when a sinkhole swallowed the container in which the workers were working. Carte Blanche investigates who is ultimately responsible and why the mine has not reopened yet.
Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein | Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


Near Barberton, Mpumalanga is Lily Gold mine. It was here 4 years ago the mine collapsed, burying 3 employees - Solomon Nyirenda, Pretty Nkambule and Yvonne Mnisi. But they have not been forgotten.
Master: “We are here for our brothers and sisters, they died and nothing is being done. I’m black and no one is going to bring this back but us.”
In a last-ditch, desperate attempt to find closure, and perhaps retrieve bodies for a dignified burial... colleagues of the three miners are risking their lives, entering a highly unstable mine, to try and see if they can succeed where rescuers failed.
Master: “ We think the container is there, behind this rock… God decides if we die or not. We pray every time before we come here.”
This is illegal, but the groups leader ex-mine employee Harry Mazibuko explains why it’s necessary.
Masa: Do you consider yourself a criminal Harry?
Harry: We are law abiding citizens. but for three years, now its four years, how long must we wait? But only one man, McChesney is holding people hostage. I think because maybe he’s scared of prosecution.”
Mazibuko believes Mike McChesney, CEO of Vantage Goldfields which owns LIly is responsible for the accident.
The mine opened in 2000, originally an open cast operation, they later filled the pit and it became an underground mine - roughly half a kilometre deep - with 13 levels, and a 15m thick main stability pillar called the crown pillar.
On February 5, 2016 at approximately 08:10am, a portion of the crown pillar collapsed underground. Causing a 27m long sinkhole that swallowed a container - known as the lamp room - which Pretty, Solomon and Yvonne were working in.
Muzi Vilakazi: “We heard a loud noise, and there was dust everywhere.”
Shift boss Jan Haywood, says Pretty wasn’t meant to be working that day.
Jan: she swapped, pretty swapped shifts with another girl and she died. That was a very very very sad story.
Jan: You know it's just not to say that you're a man and you're a miner you're supposed to be hard and all but to know people. Yeah just difficult was was difficult.
After the dust settled, another 76 miners found themselves trapped.
Muzi: I was very worried, and thought that we are already dead.
MCC: That was the worst day of my life within half an hour is on mine site with all the management team.
Hours after the collapse rescue teams used this air ventilation shaft to rescue all the other miners.
Busisiwe Mkhabela: ‘What hurts me the most is even now there are three people underground have not been found yet. Which means that if we weren’t able to escape then we would also be stuck underground till today.”
But the container - similar to this one - would be harder to find.
Jan: They had a response from inside, so they heard knocking sounds for a while.
Rescue teams made several attempts to get to the container, but the days turned into weeks… and months later the mine was declared too unsafe, and the rescue was called off.
MCC: We realized that there was just no hope of recovering them.
A year later the Department of Mineral Resources - DMR - held an inquiry into Lily’s collapse - a vital step provided for by the Mine Health and Safety Act to gather evidence on who, ultimately, carries blame...and what should be done. We obtained exclusive access to the report that was never published. The DMR’s Director General Thabo Mokoena said Lily’s management contravened the Mine Health and Safety Act, repeatedly. And never fixed the problems.
Mokoena: “The first incident occurred in 2009 when there was a sidewall collapse, CEO, COO and GM they admitted that they did not report that to the department.”
The DMR found that there had been at least 10 other collapses prior to the fatal accident.
Mokoena: Also in to 2013 massive sill pillar collapse. And it also failed to report that to the department. That is a contravention of the act.
Most damningly, the essential crown pillar was never supported.
Harry: what do you think the pressure are of over 41 metres of back-fill is? We were fortunate enough, because many people should have been buried there.”
MCC: The recommendations are that the law should be changed In that no infrastructure should be placed on top of a crown pillar in future.
Jan: “Safety wasn't a big thing its all about get the gold out, production production production.”
The DMR’s damning recommendation was clear -- those who called the shots, should be prosecuted. It recommended names to the NPA for charges to be instituted.
Mokoena: The executive management of the mine must be prosecuted.”
But the NPA told us that its Occupational Health and Safety prosecutors are waiting for the missing mine workers to be declared deceased...and the investigation is still ongoing. An inquest would have to be held. In the meantime, without bodies, the process is stuck. But a legal expert we consulted says a death certificate isn’t a necessity, and that prosecutors could have laid charges.
Masa: Do you think there should be any prosecutions. People have died
I don't believe they should.
Masa: Don't you think it's a bit disingenuous to say that no one can take responsibility. I mean you are the CEO?
MCC: I am and the company takes accountability and responsibility.We stay within the law.
Masa: Prior to this it seems you weren't you know you contradicted the Health and Safety Act. And that report clearly states that. So you've had a change of heart.
MCC: No we haven't had a change of heart. I've never had a fatality in my nearly 40 year career until these three people died. we've always been one of the safest mines.So that's absolutely nonsense.
Masa Well it can't be complete nonsense. It can't be an accident if you had ten collapses before and you never reported them. There are collapses in every mine every day. But you are obligated as they only added to report them?
McChesney: and you need to ask The two managers who never reported the three out of the 10 accidents
Masa: that’s one too many.
McChesney: Yes of course it's one too many.
Masa: It's not absolute nonsense because the writings were seemingly on the wall.
MCC: That's your opinion. It happened. Things happen in mining. And I'm very sorry it happened. I’m desperately sorry it happened.
Possibly the DMR’s most devastating finding is that the remains MAY never be recovered.
This has shattered, Solomon’s mother Fiona Nyirenda, Pretty’s Mother, Beauty Masilane, and Yvonne’s father Elmon Mnisi.
Elmon: My closure would be that we find her dead or alive. So without finding them All three of them Solomon and pretty, nothing will change, until i die.
Fiona: I hear people say that they are dead, But I don’t believe that.I’ll see him.
Beauty: My daughter left 5 month old child. IIts better if you can see the body, now we don’t know where they are? If they’re clothed, What they eating? Or what are in condition they are in, we don’t know. Its driving us insane.
Meanwhile McChesney says he’s keen for the mine to reopen speedily - as it’s been haemorrhaging money and the bills keep piling up.
Mcc: I put the company into business rescue as a result of the fact that we had no means of income.
LINK: TO ADD INSULT TO INJURY, THE BUSINESS RESCUE PROCESS HAS BEEN MIRED IN LEGAL BATTLES AS MCCHESNEY AND A POTENTIAL BUYER, MINING ENTREPRENEUR FRED ARENDSE AND HIS COMPANY FLAMING SILVER HAVE LOCKED HORNS OVER AN APPARENT LACK OF FUNDING.
CEO of Flaming Silver Fred Arendse has 28 years of experience in the mining industry. He wants to buy the mine and has a plan to reopen it.
Arendse: “To both go back into gold bearing areas, that way you can employ people, but at the same time retrieve the container.”
MCC: “We signed an agreement with Flaming silver, and he promised the money within 90 days..”
But 17 months later McChesney says, Arendse hadn’t produced the money.
Fred: “That's a complete lie, the narrative by vantage says we don’t have the money, let me tell you why he doesn't want to believe that. McChesney made another deal with another group while we have a contract.”
LINK: THE LEGAL BATTLES ASIDE, THE DMR SANCTIONED ARENDSE’S FLAMING SILVER TO TAKE OVER THE MINE...BUT MCCHESNEY AND THE BUSINESS RESCUE PRACTITIONER, STILL NOT SATISFIED WITH ARENDSE’S AVAILABLE FUNDING, LOOKED FOR ANOTHER BUYER, WHO WOULD PAY MORE.
Rob Devereux, the business rescue practitioner, says he couldn’t implement the rescue plan because of the legal delays.
ROB: the law is very specific. You have one plan. That people vote on it you implement it. And there’s case law to say that you can't change a plan without a lot of consent.
But a Judge forced Devereaux to amend the rescue plan. McChesney is appealing the judgement.
LINK: AND NOW ARENDSE HAS PUT IN A SECOND OFFER TO PURCHASE THE MINE IN ANOTHER CONSORTIUM...EFFECTIVELY UPPING PRESSURE ON THE MINE TO OPEN BY BUYING IT’S 400 MILLION RAND DEBT FROM THE BANK, MAKING IT THE MINES BIGGEST CREDITOR.
Lily Mine still has ten years of viable gold left inside, but its closure has split the community - some support McChesney and others Arendse. Crippled by desperate unemployment, the community has little time for these corporate battles. So, the families and miners have made it harder to be ignored by camping nearby the mine’s entrance.
Harry: We started this camp on that April 20 19 because it was over three years and there's not developments regarding the recruitment of the container.
In the meantime, the unemployed miners rely on donations - like those from Arendse and others…
Arendse: “I paid for their schooling, uniforms, stationary, and for a counsellor to be sent up there, so that the families can start dealing with this.”
LINK: DEVEREUX FEARS LIQUIDATION MAY BE THE ONLY WAY FORWARD - AND THAT MAY TAKE SEVERAL YEARS TO THE DETRIMENT OF THE FAMILIES AND MINERS. BUT THE DMR ARE PRESSURING THE PARTIES TO SETTLE, BECAUSE FOUR YEARS IS JUST TOO LONG.
Mokoena: “We met with McChesney and the BRP we told them that gentlemen we have to make sure that this matter is resolved I think we will be able to arrive at an amicable settlement.”
Beauty: “I beg that they help us retrieve our children, If they could rescue them we can find peace. That’s all. so that we can find peace. If they can just rescue them so we can find peace.

Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 04 February 2020 Press Release: The anatomy of a mine collapse – what happened at Lily Mine? It’s been four years of waiting in agony for the families of the three miners who never made it out of the collapsed Lily Mine in Barberton, Mpumalanga. Meanwhile, the Department of Mineral Resources has reached damning conclusions in an unpublished report into events and oversights that preceded the fatal collapse, when a sinkhole swallowed the container in which the workers were working. Carte Blanche investigates who is ultimately responsible and why the mine has not reopened yet. Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein | Presenter: Masa Kekana Script: Near Barberton, Mpumalanga is Lily Gold mine. It was here 4 years ago the mine collapsed, burying 3 employees - Solomon Nyirenda, Pretty Nkambule and Yvonne Mnisi. But they have not been forgotten. Master: “We are here for our brothers and sisters, they died and nothing is being done. I’m black and no one is going to bring this back but us.” In a last-ditch, desperate attempt to find closure, and perhaps retrieve bodies for a dignified burial... colleagues of the three miners are risking their lives, entering a highly unstable mine, to try and see if they can succeed where rescuers failed. Master: “ We think the container is there, behind this rock… God decides if we die or not. We pray every time before we come here.” This is illegal, but the groups leader ex-mine employee Harry Mazibuko explains why it’s necessary. Masa: Do you consider yourself a criminal Harry? Harry: We are law abiding citizens. but for three years, now its four years, how long must we wait? But only one man, McChesney is holding people hostage. I think because maybe he’s scared of prosecution.” Mazibuko believes Mike McChesney, CEO of Vantage Goldfields which owns LIly is responsible for the accident. The mine opened in 2000, originally an open cast operation, they later filled the pit and it became an underground mine - roughly half a kilometre deep - with 13 levels, and a 15m thick main stability pillar called the crown pillar. On February 5, 2016 at approximately 08:10am, a portion of the crown pillar collapsed underground. Causing a 27m long sinkhole that swallowed a container - known as the lamp room - which Pretty, Solomon and Yvonne were working in. Muzi Vilakazi: “We heard a loud noise, and there was dust everywhere.” Shift boss Jan Haywood, says Pretty wasn’t meant to be working that day. Jan: she swapped, pretty swapped shifts with another girl and she died. That was a very very very sad story. Jan: You know it's just not to say that you're a man and you're a miner you're supposed to be hard and all but to know people. Yeah just difficult was was difficult. After the dust settled, another 76 miners found themselves trapped. Muzi: I was very worried, and thought that we are already dead. MCC: That was the worst day of my life within half an hour is on mine site with all the management team. Hours after the collapse rescue teams used this air ventilation shaft to rescue all the other miners. Busisiwe Mkhabela: ‘What hurts me the most is even now there are three people underground have not been found yet. Which means that if we weren’t able to escape then we would also be stuck underground till today.” But the container - similar to this one - would be harder to find. Jan: They had a response from inside, so they heard knocking sounds for a while. Rescue teams made several attempts to get to the container, but the days turned into weeks… and months later the mine was declared too unsafe, and the rescue was called off. MCC: We realized that there was just no hope of recovering them. A year later the Department of Mineral Resources - DMR - held an inquiry into Lily’s collapse - a vital step provided for by the Mine Health and Safety Act to gather evidence on who, ultimately, carries blame...and what should be done. We obtained exclusive access to the report that was never published. The DMR’s Director General Thabo Mokoena said Lily’s management contravened the Mine Health and Safety Act, repeatedly. And never fixed the problems. Mokoena: “The first incident occurred in 2009 when there was a sidewall collapse, CEO, COO and GM they admitted that they did not report that to the department.” The DMR found that there had been at least 10 other collapses prior to the fatal accident. Mokoena: Also in to 2013 massive sill pillar collapse. And it also failed to report that to the department. That is a contravention of the act. Most damningly, the essential crown pillar was never supported. Harry: what do you think the pressure are of over 41 metres of back-fill is? We were fortunate enough, because many people should have been buried there.” MCC: The recommendations are that the law should be changed In that no infrastructure should be placed on top of a crown pillar in future. Jan: “Safety wasn't a big thing its all about get the gold out, production production production.” The DMR’s damning recommendation was clear -- those who called the shots, should be prosecuted. It recommended names to the NPA for charges to be instituted. Mokoena: The executive management of the mine must be prosecuted.” But the NPA told us that its Occupational Health and Safety prosecutors are waiting for the missing mine workers to be declared deceased...and the investigation is still ongoing. An inquest would have to be held. In the meantime, without bodies, the process is stuck. But a legal expert we consulted says a death certificate isn’t a necessity, and that prosecutors could have laid charges. Masa: Do you think there should be any prosecutions. People have died I don't believe they should. Masa: Don't you think it's a bit disingenuous to say that no one can take responsibility. I mean you are the CEO? MCC: I am and the company takes accountability and responsibility.We stay within the law. Masa: Prior to this it seems you weren't you know you contradicted the Health and Safety Act. And that report clearly states that. So you've had a change of heart. MCC: No we haven't had a change of heart. I've never had a fatality in my nearly 40 year career until these three people died. we've always been one of the safest mines.So that's absolutely nonsense. Masa Well it can't be complete nonsense. It can't be an accident if you had ten collapses before and you never reported them. There are collapses in every mine every day. But you are obligated as they only added to report them? McChesney: and you need to ask The two managers who never reported the three out of the 10 accidents Masa: that’s one too many. McChesney: Yes of course it's one too many. Masa: It's not absolute nonsense because the writings were seemingly on the wall. MCC: That's your opinion. It happened. Things happen in mining. And I'm very sorry it happened. I’m desperately sorry it happened. Possibly the DMR’s most devastating finding is that the remains MAY never be recovered. This has shattered, Solomon’s mother Fiona Nyirenda, Pretty’s Mother, Beauty Masilane, and Yvonne’s father Elmon Mnisi. Elmon: My closure would be that we find her dead or alive. So without finding them All three of them Solomon and pretty, nothing will change, until i die. Fiona: I hear people say that they are dead, But I don’t believe that.I’ll see him. Beauty: My daughter left 5 month old child. IIts better if you can see the body, now we don’t know where they are? If they’re clothed, What they eating? Or what are in condition they are in, we don’t know. Its driving us insane. Meanwhile McChesney says he’s keen for the mine to reopen speedily - as it’s been haemorrhaging money and the bills keep piling up. Mcc: I put the company into business rescue as a result of the fact that we had no means of income. LINK: TO ADD INSULT TO INJURY, THE BUSINESS RESCUE PROCESS HAS BEEN MIRED IN LEGAL BATTLES AS MCCHESNEY AND A POTENTIAL BUYER, MINING ENTREPRENEUR FRED ARENDSE AND HIS COMPANY FLAMING SILVER HAVE LOCKED HORNS OVER AN APPARENT LACK OF FUNDING. CEO of Flaming Silver Fred Arendse has 28 years of experience in the mining industry. He wants to buy the mine and has a plan to reopen it. Arendse: “To both go back into gold bearing areas, that way you can employ people, but at the same time retrieve the container.” MCC: “We signed an agreement with Flaming silver, and he promised the money within 90 days..” But 17 months later McChesney says, Arendse hadn’t produced the money. Fred: “That's a complete lie, the narrative by vantage says we don’t have the money, let me tell you why he doesn't want to believe that. McChesney made another deal with another group while we have a contract.” LINK: THE LEGAL BATTLES ASIDE, THE DMR SANCTIONED ARENDSE’S FLAMING SILVER TO TAKE OVER THE MINE...BUT MCCHESNEY AND THE BUSINESS RESCUE PRACTITIONER, STILL NOT SATISFIED WITH ARENDSE’S AVAILABLE FUNDING, LOOKED FOR ANOTHER BUYER, WHO WOULD PAY MORE. Rob Devereux, the business rescue practitioner, says he couldn’t implement the rescue plan because of the legal delays. ROB: the law is very specific. You have one plan. That people vote on it you implement it. And there’s case law to say that you can't change a plan without a lot of consent. But a Judge forced Devereaux to amend the rescue plan. McChesney is appealing the judgement. LINK: AND NOW ARENDSE HAS PUT IN A SECOND OFFER TO PURCHASE THE MINE IN ANOTHER CONSORTIUM...EFFECTIVELY UPPING PRESSURE ON THE MINE TO OPEN BY BUYING IT’S 400 MILLION RAND DEBT FROM THE BANK, MAKING IT THE MINES BIGGEST CREDITOR. Lily Mine still has ten years of viable gold left inside, but its closure has split the community - some support McChesney and others Arendse. Crippled by desperate unemployment, the community has little time for these corporate battles. So, the families and miners have made it harder to be ignored by camping nearby the mine’s entrance. Harry: We started this camp on that April 20 19 because it was over three years and there's not developments regarding the recruitment of the container. In the meantime, the unemployed miners rely on donations - like those from Arendse and others… Arendse: “I paid for their schooling, uniforms, stationary, and for a counsellor to be sent up there, so that the families can start dealing with this.” LINK: DEVEREUX FEARS LIQUIDATION MAY BE THE ONLY WAY FORWARD - AND THAT MAY TAKE SEVERAL YEARS TO THE DETRIMENT OF THE FAMILIES AND MINERS. BUT THE DMR ARE PRESSURING THE PARTIES TO SETTLE, BECAUSE FOUR YEARS IS JUST TOO LONG. Mokoena: “We met with McChesney and the BRP we told them that gentlemen we have to make sure that this matter is resolved I think we will be able to arrive at an amicable settlement.” Beauty: “I beg that they help us retrieve our children, If they could rescue them we can find peace. That’s all. so that we can find peace. If they can just rescue them so we can find peace.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): 3 people went in, and never came out. But what happened and how did it happen and what will happen next? Carte Blanche has exclusive access and will bring you shocking information 4 years on.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have the miners. We have background sources. We have the documents necessary to show what happened on the day. We have amazing footage from the miners themselves, and those on the ground at the time. We also have amazing interviews with those that were there, and first hand accounts from family members of the victims. It's been 4 years, but the 3 victims are still down there - and from our documents it's likely they will never be recovered. We will answer, how this happened, examine the evidence and find out why this happened.

Audio: depending on length of insert – could be 20 minutes, but obviously depends on what we have. It will be an epic – really could be a doccie. For now we have the DMR report that nails the managers. We have sources at the mine that have been camping there – we can hear what’s been happening, the effort to help minors. We have our main source going on camera, and then we have the family members (3 families). We have the survivor stories, we have the stories of the town and how it’s failed. We have confronts with Mike McChesney to do, intv with DMR. ROR from rescue practitioners, others named in report. We have the graphic and to explain the years before the accident and the mess it’s been left in since. 2. Lily mine: I had asked you for feedback if I can send a camera man to interview Jan Haywood – the former mine shift leader who was cited in the report, and testified at the commission. He has the entire story, and can give us everything in detail on camera. It would cost R2,500 + petrol for camera man to go there and interview him? It’s R100km roughly from Durban. And Duncan Grant would film for me. As I doubt we would pay for me to go there, I can only skype him, and I think as someone who is speaking on the record it would be first prize to get this interview now and lock it down before they change their mind.
